accepted.s: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 primarily seeks to:
o: Control the use of genetically modified organisms
Protect forests and wildlife through protected-area management
Regulate only the discharge of industrial effluents into rivers
Prevent, control and abate air pollution and maintain air-quality standards
accepted.x: The principal objective of the Air Act is to prevent, control and abate air pollution and to maintain prescribed air-quality standards.
accepted.tq: Identify the precise statutory purpose rather than a related environmental objective.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Air Act, 1981:
1. It came into force on 16 May 1981.
2. It consists of seven chapters and 54 sections.
3. It was modelled on the Water Act, 1974.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The Air Act came into force on 16 May 1981, contains seven chapters and 54 sections, and was modelled on the Water Act.
accepted.tq: Split the options by checking the date, structure and legislative relationship separately.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following was specifically added to the definition of ‘air pollutant’ by the 1987 amendment to the Air Act?
accepted.x: The 1987 amendment expanded the definition of air pollutant to include noise.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the statutory definition of air pollutant and other environmental pollutants.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Who is empowered to declare an area as an air pollution control area under the Air Act, 1981?
accepted.x: The State Government may declare an air pollution control area under Chapter IV, particularly Sections 19 to 31, of the Air Act.
accepted.tq: Use the ‘who would do this job?’ method to identify the competent authority.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Section 31A of the Air Act, 1981 is associated with the power to:
o: Give directions for enforcement of the Act
Collect water cess from local authorities
accepted.x: Section 31A empowers the pollution control authorities to issue directions, including directions connected with enforcement and environmental compensation.
accepted.tq: Match the section number with its distinctive statutory power.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The CPCB was already in existence under the Water Act before it was assigned functions under the Air Act.
2. State Pollution Control Boards enforce the provisions of the Air Act at the State level.
3. The Air Act created an entirely separate set of Central and State Boards unrelated to the Water Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The CPCB, originally established under the Water Act, was assigned air-pollution functions, while SPCBs enforce the Act in the States. Statement 3 is false because the same board structure was used.
accepted.tq: Spot the wrong statement that reverses the institutional relationship between the two Acts.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the Water Act, 1974 from the Air Act, 1981?
o: The Water Act has eight chapters and 64 sections, whereas the Air Act has seven chapters and 54 sections.
The Water Act has seven chapters and 54 sections, whereas the Air Act has eight chapters and 64 sections.
Both Acts have eight chapters and 64 sections.
Both Acts have seven chapters and 54 sections.
accepted.x: The Water Act contains eight chapters and 64 sections; the Air Act contains seven chapters and 54 sections.
accepted.tq: Compare the numerical structure of the two statutes without reversing the columns.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Act)
a. Water Act, 1974
b. Air Act, 1981
c. Water Cess Act, 1977

d. Air Act amendment, 1987

List-II (Feature)
i. Inclusion of noise in the definition of air pollutant
 ii. Cess on water consumed by specified industries and local authorities
 iii. Standards for discharge of effluents
 iv. Declaration of air pollution control areas and emission standards

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
accepted.x: The Water Act deals with effluent-discharge standards; the Air Act deals with air-control areas and emissions; the Cess Act funds the Boards; and the 1987 amendment added noise.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes containing a reversed statutory feature.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following is a common requirement under both the Water Act, 1974 and the Air Act, 1981?
o: Compulsory registration under the Water Cess Act
Declaration of every industrial site as an air pollution control area
Prior consent of the concerned Board to establish and operate a polluting unit
Prior approval of the National Green Tribunal for every industrial unit
accepted.x: Both Acts require prior consent of the Pollution Control Board for establishing and operating a unit that may cause pollution.
accepted.tq: Find the common legal mechanism rather than a feature belonging exclusively to one Act.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The power of Pollution Control Boards to levy environmental compensation under Section 31A of the Air Act and Section 33A of the Water Act was upheld subject to which limitation?
o: It may be exercised without any connection to actual or imminent harm.
It may be exercised only against government-owned industries.
It may be exercised only when environmental harm is clear or imminent.
It may be exercised only after a criminal conviction.
accepted.x: The power to levy compensation has been upheld, but its exercise must be connected with clear or imminent environmental harm.
accepted.tq: Apply the legal power to a fact pattern while checking the limiting condition.
accepted.sec: Air Act 1981 - purpose, noise, air pollution control areas  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 is regarded as India’s first:
accepted.x: The Water Act, 1974 is regarded as India’s first pollution-control law and focuses on preventing and controlling water pollution.
accepted.tq: Recall the distinctive historical position of the statute among environmental laws.
accepted.sec: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Water Act, 1974 was enacted under Article 252 of the Constitution. What is the implication of this arrangement?
o: It applies to States that adopt it through the constitutionally prescribed process.
It can be enforced only after approval by the Supreme Court.
It automatically applies only to Union Territories.
It applies exclusively to subjects in the Union List.
accepted.x: Article 252 permits Parliament to legislate on a State subject when States adopt the required resolution; the law applies in the States adopting it.
accepted.tq: Connect the constitutional route of legislation with its territorial application.
accepted.sec: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which body was renamed the Central Pollution Control Board by the 1988 amendment to the Water Act?
o: Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution
accepted.x: The Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution, created in 1974, was renamed the CPCB by the 1988 amendment.
accepted.tq: Use the predecessor-to-present-name relationship to avoid confusing neighbouring water institutions.
accepted.sec: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Before discharging effluents, an industry generally requires:
1. Consent to establish from the State Pollution Control Board
2. Consent to operate from the State Pollution Control Board
3. Permission only from the National Green Tribunal

Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Industries require consent to establish and consent to operate from the SPCB before discharging effluents. Permission only from the NGT is not the statutory consent mechanism.
accepted.tq: Reject the wrong-authority trap by identifying the body that grants operational consent.
accepted.sec: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 was intended primarily to:
o: Raise funds for the Pollution Control Boards through a cess on specified water consumption
Replace the consent mechanism under the Water Act
Impose a cess exclusively on agricultural land holdings
accepted.x: The Cess Act imposed a cess on water consumed by specified industries and local authorities to finance the activities of the Boards.
accepted.tq: Identify the funding purpose and reject unrelated environmental-finance functions.
accepted.sec: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Under the Water Cess Act, a rebate of 25 per cent was available for installing:
accepted.x: The Water Cess Act provided a 25 per cent rebate for installing treatment plants, encouraging reduction and treatment of polluted discharges.
accepted.tq: Link the numerical rebate with the specific compliance measure it encouraged.
accepted.sec: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977:
1. Its proceeds were credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.
2. It contained 17 sections.
3. It was subsumed or repealed in connection with the introduction of GST in 2017.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The Cess Act had 17 sections, its proceeds went to the Consolidated Fund of India, and it was subsumed or repealed with the GST framework in 2017.
accepted.tq: Check each independent statutory detail before selecting the coded combination.
accepted.sec: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
accepted.x: The Water Rules were made in 1975, while the Cess Rules were made in 1978.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the close years attached to the Water Rules and Cess Rules.
accepted.sec: Water Act 1974 - purpose, boards, consent, Cess Act link  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The ‘polluter pays’ principle means that:
o: Pollution is permissible if compensation is paid in advance.
The State must bear all costs of environmental restoration irrespective of the polluter.
Only affected residents must finance environmental restoration.
The person or company responsible for pollution bears the cost of repairing the resulting damage.
accepted.x: Under the polluter-pays principle, the responsible person or company bears the cost of repairing environmental damage caused by the pollution.
accepted.tq: Apply the exact meaning of a legal principle to the responsible party and the remedial cost.
accepted.sec: Judicial principles → case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which case is associated with the introduction of both the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle into Indian environmental law?
o: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India
M.C. Mehta v Union of India concerning the Oleum gas leak
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v Union of India
accepted.x: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v Union of India, decided in 1996, is associated with both the precautionary and polluter-pays principles. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action reaffirmed polluter pays.
accepted.tq: Use the case-principle association rather than matching all cases by environmental subject alone.
accepted.sec: Judicial principles → case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Under the precautionary principle, environmental harm should be prevented:
o: Only when the developer voluntarily accepts liability
Only after the harm has become irreversible
Only when a criminal court first establishes negligence
Even when complete scientific certainty about the harm is unavailable
accepted.x: The precautionary principle requires preventive action despite the absence of complete scientific certainty, and the burden of proof lies on the developer.
accepted.tq: Recognise the preventive logic of the principle and reject the ‘wait for certainty’ trap.
accepted.sec: Judicial principles → case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The doctrine of absolute liability for hazardous industries is associated with:
o: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v Union of India
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India
M.C. Mehta v Union of India concerning the Oleum gas leak
accepted.x: The Oleum gas leak case established absolute liability for hazardous industries, without the exceptions traditionally associated with strict liability.
accepted.tq: Match the distinctive judicial principle with the case involving hazardous industry liability.
accepted.sec: Judicial principles → case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Precautionary principle — Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v Union of India
Public trust doctrine — M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath
Absolute liability — M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath
Polluter pays — Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v Union of India
accepted.x: Absolute liability is associated with M.C. Mehta v Union of India in the Oleum gas leak case. M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath is associated with the public trust doctrine.
accepted.tq: Find the single swapped case-principle pair.
accepted.sec: Judicial principles → case  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The right to a clean and pollution-free environment has been read by the Supreme Court into:
accepted.x: The Supreme Court has interpreted the right to life under Article 21 to include the right to a healthy, clean and pollution-free environment.
accepted.tq: Identify the constitutional article through the judicially expanded right rather than its literal wording alone.
accepted.sec: Constitutional provisions - Articles 21, 48A, 51A(g)  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Article 48A of the Constitution directs the State to:
o: Establish a separate Pollution Control Board in every district
Protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife
Impose a fundamental duty on every citizen to protect rivers
Guarantee free legal aid in environmental disputes
accepted.x: Article 48A is a Directive Principle requiring the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.
accepted.tq: Separate a Directive Principle addressed to the State from a Fundamental Duty addressed to citizens.
accepted.sec: Constitutional provisions - Articles 21, 48A, 51A(g)  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which of the following is included in the Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(g)?
o: Protecting and improving the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife
Constituting the Central Pollution Control Board
accepted.x: Article 51A(g) requires citizens to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to show compassion for living creatures.
accepted.tq: Distinguish a citizen’s environmental duty from statutory functions of public authorities.
accepted.sec: Constitutional provisions - Articles 21, 48A, 51A(g)  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Articles 48A and 51A(g) were inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
2. Article 48A is a Directive Principle of State Policy.
3. Article 51A(g) is a Fundamental Duty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The 42nd Amendment inserted Article 48A as a Directive Principle and Article 51A(g) as a Fundamental Duty, both in 1976.
accepted.tq: Check the amendment, constitutional part and article classification together.
accepted.sec: Constitutional provisions - Articles 21, 48A, 51A(g)  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Assertion (A): Article 21 has been interpreted to include the right to a healthy environment.
Reason (R): The right to life under Article 21 is not confined to mere physical existence.

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
accepted.x: Both statements are true. The broad judicial interpretation of the right to life beyond mere physical existence supports inclusion of a healthy environment within Article 21.
accepted.tq: Test whether the constitutional explanation directly supports the judicial interpretation.
accepted.sec: Constitutional provisions - Articles 21, 48A, 51A(g)  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which constitutional provision has been linked by the Supreme Court with enforcement action by Pollution Control Boards?
accepted.x: The Supreme Court has linked Pollution Control Board enforcement to the citizen’s environmental duty under Article 51A(g).
accepted.tq: Use the specific constitutional linkage instead of selecting a generally environment-related provision.
accepted.sec: Constitutional provisions - Articles 21, 48A, 51A(g)  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Enactment of the Water Cess Act
B. Enactment of the Air Act
C. 42nd Constitutional Amendment inserting Articles 48A and 51A(g)
D. Amendment to the Air Act adding noise to the definition of air pollutant
accepted.x: The sequence is Water Cess Act (1977), Air Act (1981), 42nd Amendment (1976) — wait, this ordering reveals that the constitutional amendment preceded the Air Act. Therefore the correct chronological sequence is C, A, B, D.
accepted.tq: Check the dates of the middle events carefully before fixing the sequence.
accepted.sec: Constitutional provisions - Articles 21, 48A, 51A(g)  [APPSC]
